zebralogic.title: Assign fixed‑position attributes immediately
zebralogic.principle: When a clue explicitly states that a particular attribute value belongs to a specific house number, assign that value to that house right away. This prevents later contradictions and reduces the search space.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When parsing clues that mention a house index (e.g., "Alice lives in the third house").
zebralogic.example: Ignoring a clue like "Bob is in the fifth house" and placing Bob elsewhere.

zebralogic.title: Translate direct adjacency into offset constraints
zebralogic.principle: If a clue says X is directly left/right of Y, enforce that X and Y occupy adjacent houses with the correct order (X = Y‑1 for left, X = Y+1 for right).
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When parsing adjacency clues containing "directly left of" or "directly right of".
zebralogic.example: Treating "X is directly left of Y" as merely "X is somewhere left of Y" and allowing a gap between them.

zebralogic.title: Interpret distance clues correctly
zebralogic.principle: When a clue says there are N houses between X and Y, enforce that the absolute difference in positions is N + 1 (exactly N houses separating them).
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When parsing clues that specify a number of houses between two items.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting "one house between A and B" as distance 1 instead of distance 2.

zebralogic.title: Bind equivalence clues to the same house
zebralogic.principle: When a clue equates two (or more) attribute values (e.g., "The photographer has gray hair"), treat them as belonging to the same house and propagate all linked attributes together.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When parsing equivalence or "same person" clues.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the photographer to one house and the gray‑haired person to another, violating the equivalence.

zebralogic.title: Treat 'somewhere left/right of' as inequality
zebralogic.principle: Clues that say X is somewhere left/right of Y impose only an ordering (pos(X) < pos(Y) or pos(X) > pos(Y)), not adjacency. Do not force X to be directly next to Y.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When parsing ordering clues without the word "directly".
zebralogic.example: Treating "black hair is somewhere left of Bob" as "black hair is directly left of Bob" and fixing them adjacent.

zebralogic.title: Apply exclusion constraints
zebralogic.principle: When a clue forbids an attribute from a particular house (e.g., "Eric is not in the second house"), record that exclusion so the value cannot be placed there.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When parsing negative statements about positions.
zebralogic.example: Ignoring "Eric is not in the second house" and accidentally placing Eric in house 2.

zebralogic.title: Enforce uniqueness across each attribute category
zebralogic.principle: Each value in a category must appear exactly once across all houses. After assigning a value, remove it from the candidate lists of all other houses.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: After any assignment, and continuously while narrowing possibilities.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the same flower to two different houses, violating the one‑per‑category rule.

zebralogic.title: Preserve original case of attribute values
zebralogic.principle: When outputting the final solution, write each attribute value exactly as it appears in the problem statement, preserving capitalization and spelling.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: During the final formatting of the answer.
zebralogic.example: Outputting "Black" instead of the required "black" for a hair color.

zebralogic.title: Interpret 'next to each other' as bidirectional adjacency
zebralogic.principle: When a clue says X and Y are next to each other, enforce that they occupy adjacent houses, but allow either order unless another clue fixes the direction.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When parsing adjacency clues using the phrase "next to each other" or "are next to each other".
zebralogic.example: Assuming X must be left of Y when the clue only says they are next to each other, thereby discarding the valid opposite ordering.

zebralogic.title: Make forced assignments when only one candidate remains
zebralogic.principle: After applying all constraints, if a house (or an attribute) has exactly one possible remaining value, assign it immediately. This eliminates ambiguity and often resolves the puzzle without exhaustive search.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever the candidate list for a house or attribute shrinks to a single option, typically after exclusion, equivalence, or adjacency deductions.
zebralogic.example: If only Bob can occupy house 2 after ruling out Arnold and Eric, assign Bob to house 2.

zebralogic.description: Treating 'somewhere left/right of' as adjacency (directly left/right)
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model often conflates ordering clues with adjacency, assuming the two items must be adjacent.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Interpret 'somewhere left/right of' as a pure ordering constraint (pos(X) < pos(Y) or >) without requiring adjacency.

zebralogic.description: Interpreting 'N houses between' as distance N
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model mistakenly counts the number of houses separating two items as N instead of N + 1.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Remember that 'N houses between X and Y' means the positions differ by N + 1.

zebralogic.description: Ignoring equivalence clues that bind two attributes to the same house
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model treats linked attributes as independent, missing the requirement that they co‑occur.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Whenever a clue states that two attributes refer to the same person, bind them to the same house and propagate all linked values.

zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model may assign the same value to multiple houses, forgetting that each attribute value must be unique.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: After each assignment, remove that value from the candidate lists of all other houses; never assign a value twice.

zebralogic.description: Assuming a fixed direction for 'next to each other' clues
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model interprets 'X and Y are next to each other' as X being left of Y, ignoring the possibility that Y could be left of X.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Treat 'next to each other' as bidirectional adjacency; allow both possible orders unless another clue fixes the direction.
